summary:
We developed an **Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System** designed to protect astronauts during long-duration space missions. The system combines a wearable wrist monitoring device and an ESP32-S3-based cabin monitoring hub. It uses sensors such as MAX30102 for heart rate and SpO₂, MAX30205 for body temperature, MPU6050 for movement, SCD41 for CO₂, BME680 for environmental monitoring, and BG51 for radiation monitoring.
The system continuously collects health and cabin data, analyzes readings using filtering and baseline checks, and generates alerts when abnormal conditions are detected. It also stores health records locally and continues operating during communication blackouts, synchronizing data with ground control when connectivity returns.
This solution addresses the challenges of microgravity, radiation exposure, health risks, and communication delays. It is important because it supports early detection of potential health problems, improves astronaut safety, and enables more reliable health monitoring during future deep-space missions.
details:
Project Details: Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project, the Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System, is designed to continuously monitor astronauts' health and cabin environmental conditions during long-duration space missions.

The system consists of two main components: a wearable wrist monitoring device and an ESP32-S3-based cabin monitoring hub. The wearable device uses sensors to measure heart rate, blood oxygen levels, body temperature and movement. The cabin hub monitors carbon dioxide levels, pressure, environmental conditions and radiation.

The collected data is processed by the ESP32-S3, which filters sensor noise, checks readings against configured limits and compares them with the astronaut's normal health baseline. If abnormal readings are detected, the system generates local warnings or critical alerts. It also stores health records locally and continues working during communication blackouts. When communication is restored, stored information can be synchronized with ground control.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Continuous monitoring of astronaut health and cabin conditions.
  • Early identification of possible health abnormalities.
  • Immediate alerts for potentially dangerous conditions.
  • Independent operation during communication blackouts.
  • Local storage of health records for later analysis.
  • Improved awareness of environmental risks during space missions.
  • Better support for astronauts and ground medical teams.

3. What is the intended impact?

The main goal is to improve astronaut safety during long-duration missions, especially deep-space missions where immediate communication with Earth may not always be possible.

The system aims to reduce delays in identifying potential medical problems, support faster onboard responses and provide reliable health records for medical teams. It can contribute to safer future missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware and software were used?

Hardware and sensors:

  • ESP32-S3 – Main processing and control unit.
  • MAX30102 – Heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring.
  • MAX30205 – Body temperature monitoring.
  • MPU6050 – Motion and movement detection.
  • SCD41 – Carbon dioxide monitoring.
  • BME680 – Environmental monitoring and pressure-related measurements.
  • BG51 – Radiation monitoring component.

Software and technologies:

  • Embedded programming for sensor integration and data processing.
  • Kalman filtering for reducing sensor noise.
  • SQLite for local data storage.
  • ESP32-S3 firmware for processing readings and generating alerts.
  • NASA Open Spaceflight Data (OSDR) for research and understanding spaceflight health conditions.
  • NASA-STD-3001 and Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) concepts for informing system requirements and communication design.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of our project is the combination of wearable health monitoring and cabin environmental monitoring in one autonomous system.

Instead of depending entirely on continuous communication with Earth, the system can process information, identify unusual readings, alert astronauts and store important records directly onboard. Combining personal health data with environmental information provides a broader understanding of possible risks to astronauts.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Astronaut safety and health risks.
  • Radiation exposure and microgravity-related effects.
  • Reliability and accuracy of sensor readings.
  • Low-power and compact hardware requirements.
  • Communication delays and blackouts.
  • Offline processing and secure data storage.
  • Ease of use for astronauts.
  • The need for medical-specialist validation of alert thresholds and response procedures.

Overall, our project aims to make long-duration space missions safer through autonomous health monitoring, early warnings and reliable onboard data management.
